utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Mr. Bradley Sorrentino who's been with my team since June from the University of San Diego, Thomas Jefferson Law School. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's continue, General. First, just to follow-up on something you said yesterday. It's not about your statement, it's about General Krstic, talking about -- well, let me just read back what you said at page 76. "And the first information and intimations of these events I started learning after the statements of General Krstic that was disclosed in certain media in Bosnia-Herzegovina; however, I wish to note there as well that in the statement of General Krstic's the role of the protection regiment in these events was presented in a completely wrong and erroneous manner. So even then I did not know the real truth about these events." And what I want to do is read you a couple parts of General Krstic's testimony that I think you were referring to. This is his testimony in his Defence at 6330 is the page. General Krstic said --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, is there a 65 ter number for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, it's 24242, excuse me, e-court page 467. And I'll keep it short.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He said: "That is to say, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic when he returned from the area of Srebrenica and Bratunac confided in Major Golic," and he's talking about the executions. And he continues at line 16: "Later on the 12th and 13th he had taken part and had been in charge of some soldiers and units of the 65th Protection Regiment," speaking about Popovic, "and the 10th Detachment in the liquidation of prisoners in Kravica and the village of Lazete, the village of Laze in the vicinity of Bratunac." Is that something you would say is just completely not true, that the 65th Protection Regiment soldiers took part in those liquidations?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I state with full responsibility that this is completely made up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So from your knowledge, that's perjury by General Krstic? That was under oath.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he stated that under oath, but I can't [as interpreted] say that this is absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me read you one other part. This is at e-court page 471, his testimony at page 6334, General Krstic again: "The very fact that the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment took part in capturing members of the 28th Division, that they handed them over to their superior, and that was General Mladic, and that later from that protective regiment soldiers were selected to execute prisoners of war is sufficiently eloquent evidence of the responsibility of the commander of the military police of the 65th Protection Regiment, Malinic." Would you say that is also a completely false statement by General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely false, and I'm convinced that you have evidence to disprove this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Did you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Karadzic is intervening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I interrupt, although I don't want to. In line 24 of page 2 I see that the witness is recorded as saying "I can't say," however he said "I can say." That's line 24 of the provisional transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's duly noted. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you know that President Karadzic is trying to introduce this transcript into evidence for the truth of its content, General Krstic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it makes sense to introduce the entire transcript, maybe parts of it. But I was speaking about those parts of the statement that relate to the role of the protection regiment in General Krstic's statement. That part is completely made up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's go back to DutchBat just a little bit more of what we were talking about yesterday, and the -- their detention at Nova Kasaba. You said when we were finishing yesterday that it was a different unit you knew that had stopped and detained them. Let me tell you what the evidence in this case is. This is the testimony of Mr. Egbers at page 2759 of his transcript, e-court page 37, talking about where they were stopped, speaking of Mr. Malinic. "Q. And did he identify himself as being in charge of the roadblock? "A. He identified himself as being in charge of the headquarters and the things that happened on the road with his soldiers. I was stopped by his soldiers, yes." So Malinic explained to DutchBat that it was his soldiers who stopped them, not some unnamed Drina Corps unit; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that there were some inaccuracies even yesterday in connection with this unit. According to the information I received from Malinic, they arrived at the school and the barracks without being stopped and without being taken to the barracks. They tried to obtain information about the information -- about the situation in the direction of Kasaba-Konjevic Polje-Srebrenica. They wanted to know how safe that road was. Malinic was unable to give a security estimate and they decided to set off for Srebrenica. As soon as they reached the road - and I was told that they were in three vehicles at that moment - a group of soldiers, of whom we later learned that they were from the command of the Drina Corps, intercepted them and stole one vehicle from them. And with the remaining two vehicles, they returned to the school. I have no information to the effect that Malinic blocked the road, at least he never told me about it, that he stopped the vehicles and made them go elsewhere. So the first time around they came of their own accord to get information, then they left. They were robbed of their vehicle and they returned to the school where they stayed for another day or night or however long they stayed. Neither their weapons nor their means of communication were taken away from them. So there can be no mention of forcible detainment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 6 it says that the vehicle was stolen, whereas it was confiscated. And a little further down it says "robbed," however it should be "confiscated" again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, on the morning of the 13th of July on your second call with Major Malinic, when you discussed the prisoners, let me read out part of your testimony from the Popovic trial. This was at 15259. "Q. When you spoke to Major Malinic, did he make a request for reinforcements or help in controlling the prisoners?" Your answer: "Of course he did because he said there were many of them. I don't remember him giving me a figure. It's difficult to make an assessment. It later turned out and we reached a figure of 1200 people. But then all he was saying was: I have many of them, et cetera." Do you stand by that testimony, 1200 people were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the day he mentioned that figure to me. From the region of Borike I wasn't [realtime transcript read in error "was"] able to see for myself or come up with an estimate of my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You answered the question. The question was what you figured out. Okay, let me read back another part of your testimony in the Popovic trial. You told the Trial Chamber in that case that you knew all seven of the accused, and you were asked: "And you respect General Miletic; right?" This is at T15259. And your answer was, at T15261: "I respect all of them. They are my comrades in arms and I have great respect for all of them." And that's true; right? Vujadin Popovic, Ljubisa Beara, Borovcanin, the others in that case were your comrades in arms?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are my comrades in arms and some of them my friends. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you have great -- "great respect for them," right, that's what you testified to?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I guess that also goes for General Tolimir who hadn't been put on trial at that point?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but really. In line 10 it says "I was able," whereas the witness said "I was not able." Page 6, line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That seems to make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now look at some intercepts that I think you've seen before and you're aware of from the 13th of July when Malinic that day had around 1200 men in his custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have D02204, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is an intercept between persons identified as Beara, Zoka, and Lucic speaking at different times. It's at 10.09 a.m. and Beara says: "Hello Signor Lucic. How are you?" And then he says: "Do you hear me? Do you know that 400 balijas have shown up in Konjevic Polje? "Lucic: I know. And they've been rounded up and disarmed, everything. Beara -- and then Beara: "Excellent!" A little further down Beara says: "Yes, you can also those 20 something so the forces are not dispersed. Shove them all on the playground, who gives a fuck about them?" Further down he says: "Line them up in four to five rows" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could Serbian page be turned. Sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then probably the next page in Serbian. Beara says: "Hi, Zoka." Beara says: "What's new?" And then it continues. You've seen this intercept before; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is Beara talking to Zoran Malinic, Zoka, and Malinic's deputy, Lucic, right, about the prisoners at Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to another intercept now, P04670. This is again 13 July at 1400 hours. And just very quickly, it kind of matches what we were just discussing about 1200 prisoners being there. There's talk of: "I have more than a thousand." Y says again: "More than a thousand. "Where are they? "They are down there at the football stadium." And if we go to the next page probably in the Serbian, yeah, we see towards the bottom, the top on your page: "Fuck, I don't know whether to give these to them. "To whom? "To Zoka and the other one." And then: "Call Mico up there." Same question simply: This is about the prisoners on the field?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to P05380, 16.02 hours. Very simply again, now it's 1500 at the stadium at Kasaba, so the numbers have gone up a little. It says: "Where Malinic's unit is." Same topic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The topic could be the same, but I don't know who the participants are or where they got this information from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. But they're talking about Malinic's unit and 1500 gathered at the stadium, right, and it says "at the stadium in Kasaba," right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously they're talking about that, but I have no idea who is talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. I didn't ask you that, so don't worry about the questions I don't ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P05380, please -- sorry. P04945.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Same day, now it's 1730, so it's a bit later. And the participants, X and Y, X says: "Is it possible for us to send about ten buses from Bijeljina?" Y says: "Well, tell them right away to come, there's about 6.000 of them now." X: "Of military age?" Y: "Shut up, don't repeat." And then a little further down Y says: "I have three points, fuck it." Skipping down a bit. I think we need to go to the next page in the Serbian, please. "At each point there are roughly 1500 - 2.000." And then further down it says: "Have them report in Kasaba to the last -- have them report to the stadium." So again at this point the participants are talking, not just at Nova Kasaba but about a total of 6.000 prisoners in the custody of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figure of 6.000 is mentioned here. Where these locations are, I really don't know. It's probably about prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, but having been Zoran Malinic's superior and having been investigator on this case since 2009, you'll know that there were prisoner collection points that day at Sandici, Konjevic Polje, and Nova Kasaba, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P04671.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is going back in time a bit to another intercept. This is one you've seen before, sir, it's at 1405 the same day. X and Y. X: "Where is that?" Y: "Here at the football-pitch?" X: "Is it visible? Y: "Fuck, it is." X: "Brother, don't take anyone. I'll send you an urgent telegram now, don't take anyone," something "/put out of sight/" something, "a little. I'll send you the telegram now and explain it to you."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page in the Serbian. "Go ahead. "Secure it, well and you'll get it now in the telegram. Y: "Fine." X: "Cheers." "I will do nothing before that. X: "Nothing." This is 1405 on the 13th, discussing a telegram that's going to come about the football-pitch, and it says: "I will do nothing before that. "Nothing." And we already read right at the beginning of the cross-examination how in the 65th Protection Regiment nothing was done without a command, without an order. So we've got here at the football-pitch, send you a telegram now. This is you speaking with Zoran Malinic, isn't it, about a telegram that's going to be sent?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Zoran Malinic a number of times on that day mostly about prisoners of war and about UNPROFOR members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And about sending a telegram with instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, especially bearing in mind that the alleged telegram cannot reach Malinic urgently for technical reasons, and I cannot convey information to him in a timely manner. The telegram would have to travel through the Rogatica brigade to the Main Staff and from the Main Staff to Nova Kasaba by courier. That would have taken quite some time, and if it was about anything urgent, he would have taken the necessary measures too late. Finally, in later contacts with Malinic, I learned that he never received any telegram from me about the treatment of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll go over quite a lot of that in a minute. You say you don't recall, especially bearing in mind -- now the -- without getting into the details, that telegram wouldn't have to be couriered from the Main Staff to Nova Kasaba. It could have gone right to the Bratunac Brigade, couldn't it, and then have been couriered from there or to the communications facilities at Konjevic Polje. There was testimony that an intercept -- an operator, I believe, was working for the -- at Konjevic Polje -- or it could have gone to the 5th Engineering Unit which was just nearby or to the police headquarters at Nova Kasaba. Are you saying that the whole time that the military police battalion was headed and headquartered at Nova Kasaba, that they could only receive information by courier?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying, either by radio, over a radio relay communication, but a telegram had to go by courier from the Main Staff to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long does it take to go from Crna Rijeka to Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see, that's 20, 30, 45 to 50 kilometres. It would have taken about an hour in a car, taking into consideration that the road from Crna Rijeka to Han Pijesak is in bad condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So your --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So your truthful testimony is that any time a telegram with something that shouldn't be said over the radio needed to reach the 65th Protection Regiment's military police battalion, it would take an hour and come from the Main Staff by hand? That was the only way to reach them? That's what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that way, in terms of encrypted communication -- well, it's possible that the commander of the Drina Corps could have been used, but I'm not sure that that would have been shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's look at P00168. This is a document you've seen many times.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you discuss it in your statement. It's headed: "Procedure for the Treatment of War Prisoners," Command of the Main Staff, commander, Mladic, for his information; to the assistant commander for morale, Gvero, for his information; commander of the military police battalion, 65th, Zoran Malinic; order. And it says at the top "Borike at 1400 hours. "There are over" -- just about the time we saw that intercept that you said you couldn't recall if you sent a telegram. "There are over 1.000 members of the former 28 Division of the so-called BH army captured in the area of Dusanovo (Kasaba). Prisoners are under control of the military police battalion of the 65th ..." Now, that's accurate, isn't it, that's accurate information there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then it continues: "The assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the VRS Main Staff proposes the following measures ..." That's Tolimir; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Tolimir was assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've already told us, and it's in your statement, that he was in Borike sector that day. In the Borike area, let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And his -- what he writes or what it says is: "Prohibit access to all unauthorised individuals, filming and photographing prisoners. "Prohibit traffic for all UN vehicles en route Zvornik-Vlasenica ...," et cetera. "Commander of the military police battalion shall take measure to remove war prisoners from the main Milici-Zvornik road, place them somewhere indoors or in the area protected from sighting from the ground or air. "4. Once the commander of the military police battalion receives this order he shall contact General Miletic and receive from him additional orders and verify if the proposal has been approved by the commander of the Main Staff. "Commander. "Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic." And then handwritten on the bottom left: "Sent 1510 hours. "13 July. "1995." Signed Gojkovic. So this has been sent at 1510, according to the teleprinter operator, just about an hour after that intercept we saw, saying: Don't do anything until I send you a telegram; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it seems to me that that conversation took place at 1405, if I'm not mistaken. Maybe I am mistaken --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're correct --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- 1405, so this is about an hour later that it's sent. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sent, but it's a bit illogical that I first write a telegram, right? So if this telephone conversation took place at 1405, the one that was intercepted, and this practically - I don't know what to call this - this information about treatment of prisoners of war is written before that, five minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're hanging on the 1400 at the top and saying it says "1400," not "1406." Is that your point? Not 1410. Is that the point you're making?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not the point. There are several points here. If you wish, we can start --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from the heading --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, wait for the questions. All I was pointing out to you is getting you to agree that it says it was sent approximately one hour after that intercept, and we agree on that, right, that's what the teleprinter operator has written.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The teleprinter operator wrote that, and now how he wrote that is a separate story all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. We'll get into that in a minute. So this is an order by you on its face to Zoran Malinic about prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two paragraphs of this instruction, order, refer to the military police, and these two paragraphs are fully in line with the Rules of Service for the military police and the tasks of the military police --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So the answer is "yes"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated at the first and the second and during the interview with Mr. McCloskey that I do not remember this; however, if I really sent this the answer is yes. And I can explain each and every one of these paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Wait for me to ask --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even on this day I would sign --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Finish -- finish what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, here's one thing you said about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Nicholls, I didn't understand his answer. Mr. Savcic you said: "... however, if I really sent this the answer is yes ." What did you mean? Do you agree that you sent this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you have this document before you, you see that my name and surname are only typewritten. My signature is not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know where such a document could be considered at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, we all know that. My question is whether you agree that you sent this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the very outset, I've been saying that I do not remember this, but I cannot rule it out all together either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, let me see -- read you what you said when you were first shown this document by the OTP, that was in your interview in 2005, almost eight years ago, it was in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 25395 for my friends, at e-court page 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Q. Okay. So I really need you to help me with this. You think this is a document that was created falsely and placed in this Drina archive or is it something ..." Your answer: "I doubt it was falsified. I mean, to be honest, I don't know. I am closer to the truth if I say this is an authentic document, but if you'll allow me I really can't remember it." So whatever "closer to the truth" means, do you stand by that, that you said in your interview, which you told me right at the beginning you do stand by your interview? You're closer to the truth if you say this document is authentic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm the closest to the truth if I say, as I have said, that I do not remember this document. All the rest can be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you finish -- could you repeat the end of your sentence, please, the interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying I'm closest to the truth when I say that I do not remember this document. All the rest can be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, one of the things you said a moment ago was talking about how it didn't have a signature, et cetera. Let me explain to you what's in evidence in this case, what the person who remembers sending this telegram said, Mr. Danko Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is P00248 for my friends, his interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Here's what he said when he was shown this document in an interview. "The last document bears number 04258580. Could you look at it and comment on it. "A. It was sent by the IKM 65 ZMPT, sent to the commander of the GSBRS for knowledge, to the deputy of command of the general headquarters, and the commander of the military police -- excuse me, and the commander of the battalion of military police. I sent it." Have you ever spoken to Danko Gojkovic about this in your role as investigator about this document that he, as soon as he saw it, said he sent?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never talked to Mr. Gojkovic, but I was in a position to read the transcript of his testimony; and as far as I can remember, I saw there that he cannot say for sure who drafted this telegram or paper. If I'm not mistaken, please correct me, but I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, this might cut it short. Can you agree with me that it was completely unambiguous in his testimony that Danko Gojkovic said that he, in fact, received this telegram in the form we have it in and that he typed it into his teleprinter and sent it? And that after he did so, he put the date, time, and his signature?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you something else he said when you were shown this telegram the first time in your interview. This was at page 48 to 49 -- sorry, page 32. You said: "In the proposal of the measures that needs to be taken, assistant commander for intelligence and security of the Main Staff proposes as one of the measures that as well. Whether his intention was hiding them or protecting them, I really don't know, but I know that in that soccer field it is not a stadium. The things that happened there were completely opposite of what's been written here. They even made a list, they made a list, not a complete list, but they even made a list of the war prisoners. "Q. Have you seen that list? "A. I did not see the list, but there are witnesses who said that the list was taken away from Major Malinic later. And I really hope that there are someone, that there is someone who survived from there, who gave their details when the lists were made." So now do you know -- that was 2005. Do you now know whether there were any survivors from the men under -- the prisoners held by Zoran Malinic that day?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I had an opportunity, but I wasn't focused on that, to hear the testimony of a witness from Kasaba I think. Now, whether I'm mistaken or not, now was it in this case or was it in General Mladic's case? If I made a mistake, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you don't know that one man who had been at Nova Kasaba survived, KDZ045, survived mass executions at the dam? Is that the one you're thinking of? Or maybe you're thinking of KDZ333 who survived a mass execution at Branjevo Farm after being held at Nova Kasaba. Is it one of those two?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a witness who was at the football stadium at Nova Kasaba. Now, what happened to that man afterwards, now -- I mean, I really cannot say. I heard the testimony of a man who was in Nova Kasaba or I heard that testimony in part at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on. Just one second. Okay. I was looking for page 12, line 12, you said: "Finally, in later contacts with Malinic, I learned that he never received any telegram from me about the treatment of prisoners of war." That's not exactly what Zoran Malinic says under oath. In his transcript in the Tolimir case, which is 65 ter 25439, at his testimony at T15390, talking about this telegram he said he doesn't remember whether he received it. He didn't say: I know I never received it. The quote is: "From what I know, and from this point in time, I cannot say either yes or no. I don't remember if I received this telegram." When was it you talked to Mr. Malinic and he supposedly told you he never received it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had you read on, had you read the rest of Malinic's statement, everything would have been fine. I talked about this probably after Krstic's statement when, in a way, it became very topical, especially because of the completely false picture that was portrayed of the protection regiment. As far as I can remember, Malinic goes on to say that had he received this telegram he would have had to act on those orders; however, since he did not act on such orders, his conclusion is that he never received the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I read out is accurate. He's making that conclusion perhaps by speculating about what he would or would not have done; however, what he said was he didn't remember whether he received it or not, which is not what you said. You said he confirmed he never received it. That's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He confirmed unambiguously when talking to me that he never received that telegram, so it wasn't a question of saying anything alternative or possible or -- plausible or possible. He said unequivocally that he never received the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, that brings me to what he said under oath about speaking with you about the telegram, which is 65 ter 25439, e-court page 1, this is his testimony at page 15375 in 2011: "A. In the past ten years, I seldom met Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic. I don't know if we discussed this." And he's speaking about the telegram. "Actually, I cannot see -- say with 100 per cent certainty whether we discussed this document or not. I can't be certain either way." And later at e-court page 2, T15376, he said: "I said already that I don't remember discussing this document with Colonel Savcic in the past ten years."

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, he is saying he doesn't remember. I don't remember the exact time when we talked either, but it is certain that we did talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, one other point you've -- you say in your statement at paragraph 56 and you said something similar today, that the form of the telegram, P00168, is absolutely unacceptable, it's very disputable. But you testified and you've testified today about how it would have been delivered and the time delay. Let me remind you of something you said in the Popovic case. This is at T15265, 65 ter 25397, at e-court pages 118 to 119. When you were shown this document. "Do you see an indication on the left-hand bottom of that document of a time and date. "Yes, I do. "And what does that refer to? Hand it over. "Signals and communications are not my specialty. I don't know what this refers to, whether this refers to whether this -- to the moment when this document was received or transmitted. I really can't be sure. I don't know whether this means that this document was received at that time or whether it was given for encrypted or -- whether it was encrypted at that moment or transferred at a different moment for encrypting. I really don't know." And that's true, isn't it, communications are not your specialty?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communications are not my specialty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And let me just remind you of something you may have written that Mr. Gojkovic explained in his interview. He said that commun -- telegrams could not have been sent from Borike because there wasn't a teleprinter there. That's in his interview at e-court page 24. He said that documents to be sent from Borike - and remember, this is a professional throughout the war teleprinter operator of the brigade - that orders -- documents to be sent from Borike came to the Rogatica Brigade and his section via telephone or courier and that the IKM in Borike was about 18 kilometres from the Rogatica Brigade. And he testified, which you would have read, at T10728, that he received the telegram maybe half an hour before the time indicated as transmission time maybe, maybe 1410. So that's why there's a delay, sir. It's not because it has to come from the General Staff, from Crna Rijeka. The telegram had to be driven 18 kilometres to the Rogatica Brigade, handed to Danko Gojkovic, and then he had to type it into his teleprinter. That's why it says "1510"; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for the additional explanations that I had not been aware of. And this has to do with the following. At the forward command post of Borike, there was not a teleprinter. The encryption of documents took place in Rogatica. Quite frankly, I did not know that. Secondly, there is a misunderstanding here; that is to say, I was saying that the telegram that had been encrypted at the Rogatica Brigade, irrespective of the location, whether it's Borike -- I see that it's Rogatica here. So from that place, it has to go to the encryption of the Main Staff, and then as a telegram it is sent to the unit because it is sent to the Main Staff. I am speaking about the further sending of the telegram from the Main Staff to the battalion of the military police. It seems that we are not understanding each other because you say that this time was needed to get to the Rogatica Brigade for the telegram to get encrypted and then to be sent. That's all right. But we have this time of an hour and a half or so where we should not be referring to the Main Staff because it does not appear there yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The intercept -- sorry, the teleprinter operator stated, and I already read this out to you, he's a communications expert, you're not, that it was sent to the commander of the Main Staff for knowledge, to the deputy of command, and the commander of the battalion of the military police. That's where he says he sent it.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with the first two statements because all members of the Main Staff use single encryption. I do not agree with the other thing because the protection regiment did not have encryption of their own. They used the encryption of the Main Staff or of the unit on -- in whose area they were. So the telegram for the battalion of the military police could not have arrived through communications equipment to Nova Kasaba; rather, it had to go to the Main Staff. And then once it is deciphered, it had to be couriered to Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then they would receive it and act on it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P04407.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is 13th July 1995 from General Mladic. You can see the distribution list. Prevention of leakage of confidential military information. It's an order. And if you look at - I won't go through it all because of the time - you'll agree with me if you look at points 4 and 5 that they relate very closely to the telegram which was sent to General Mladic for approval?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. What was it that was sent to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. P00168, which I don't want to bring up again, is the telegram we've been discussing, the one that has your name on it. And what I'm asking you is if you look at point 4: "In the area of combat operations in the wider areas of Srebrenica and Zepa, prevent the entry of all local and foreign journalists, except the journalists of the Main Staff of the VRS ..." That relates to virtually very closely to the telegram of preventing access of unauthorised individuals and filming of prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it is not surprising because in all the rules that were used by the Army of Republika Srpska, from the level of the brigade, the corps, and further up, these are measures envisaged within the framework of securing the area of combat. They are regularly applied in all combat operations. We even apply them in peace time during military manoeuvres. All the militaries of the world applied the same thing whenever there is an operation or whenever they have manoeuvres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it's also not surprising when it follows a telegram sent to Mladic by General Tolimir recommending exactly that procedure; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not surprising at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P05101, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think you've seen this document before. Very quickly, it's the 14th of July, the next day, from General Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And it's informing that: "There is an unmanned aircraft in the air-space reconnoitring and jamming radio communications. Since the aircraft has been there since 0500 this morning and has probably taken pictures of certain features and movements, the following needs to be done." And one of those following is to destroy the aircraft. So my only question is at this point the VRS at the very top is aware that there were aircraft above, probably taking aerial photos; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS knew even before that that there was aircraft that was taking aerial photos. Personally, I felt their work and indirectly I their -- I felt their work activity. What General Tolimir proposes is a classical measure of anti-aircraft defence. Under paragraph 4 he says: "If spotted, the unmanned aircraft should be immediately destroyed." This means that we should engage in an anti-aircraft combat, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at your order from the next day, 65 ter 03841, signed by your deputy Jovo Lazic -- Jazic, excuse me. It's an order been preventing the leakage of confidential military information. "Order: "1. ... prevent entry of all uninvited persons into the zone of combat operations and the unit's zone of responsibility." "2," very similar to Mladic's order we just looked at: "In the zone of combat operations in the wider area of Srebrenica and Zepa, prevent the entry of all local and foreign journalists, except ...those from the Main Staff." "3. Prohibit and prevent release of information, announcements, and statements to the media about the progress, state, and results of combat operations in this area, and the overall activities carried out in the area, especially the information regarding prisoners of war, evacuated civilians, escapees, and similar." So this is your order; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not my order. You said it yourself, that this was signed by the Chief of Staff, Jovo Jazic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, when he signs under your name, isn't it with your authorisation?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. What escapees are you talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't find this. Under what number is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the end of the last sentence of number 3 -- well, there's only one sentence. It's under number 3.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it now. I suppose what he had in mind the persons that were crossing the territory. I don't know. I did not draft this order. Perhaps this was copied from the previous order by the commander of the staff. Let me ask you something: That order by Mladic was written on the 14th. We were in Crna Rijeka, some 3- to 400 metres from the command post of the Main Staff, and it took two to three days for this telegram to reach the regiment command. And I already spoke about our problem with communications, especially the encrypted telegrams. You can see that this is a copy of a previous order. I didn't have anything to do with Srebrenica. I couldn't take any measures. I couldn't carry out any activities in the Zepa sector. There were 30 soldiers with me plus --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the motorised battalion --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that manned positions facing Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I think you made your point there. Are you seriously saying that escapees here is referring to the Muslim column moving through the woods? Is that what you were trying to say? I thought those were enemy units.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? It's very difficult to interpret what somebody said when they said something or wrote something. I don't know what this person meant. Throughout the war on that note almost every day it happened that individuals or small groups left Srebrenica to go towards Kladanj and Tuzla. I don't know whether this is what is meant under this bullet point. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it says -- part of what is supposed to be prevented is information about overall activities carried out in area, especially the information regarding prisoners of war. Now, on the 15th of July, 1995, in the area, prisoners of war were being executed by the hundreds and hundreds, over a thousand of them in Kozluk. That's what this order is about keeping secret, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. I believe that Kozluk was excluded from the area to which this applies, but I would like us to look at the roles of the brigades. And you will see the application of security measures for combat. It clearly states that the commander has to take measures in order to provide for the counter-intelligence of its units --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the situation in the unit, plans, intentions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Other than these days in July 1995 and the orders we've looked at, can you show me an order that has the same language about keeping secrets about what's going on with prisoners of war and escapees, if it's so standard?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it, but I'm sure you have the order of the commander of the Drina Corps for Krivaja 95 operation, the orders of the brigade commanders. Within the bullet point order for securing combat, they had to do it. Every rule demands that. I repeat, in peace time during manoeuvres, similar measures were applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uninvited persons cannot just turn up in an area where combat is taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you telling me Krivaja says prohibit and prevent release of information about prisoners of war, that it has that language in it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I am saying that there is the wording "securing combat operation zones." Do not twist my words. I'm saying that there is a bullet point under which one has to provide for the security of a combat operations zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I have 15 minutes left of my allotted time. I'd ask for about 20 to 30 minutes, and whether I'm granted that or not depends on what I do in the next 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the areas you would like to cover for the remainder of your time if extended?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If extended, I would like to go - it may be less - into his role as an investigator for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I haven't checked the time yet, but you'll have extra 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, just a second. Could you finish in 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, try to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think -- I thought I had 15 minutes left from this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have four minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Our numbers don't match, Your Honour. I'm not doubting you, but I was -- our count was that I had 15 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have to say that I'm counting about the same as Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was -- misread the note. You have 24 minutes left. So you have about 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to be as quick as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, one of the things you say in your statement at paragraph 70 is you believe the Geneva Conventions prohibit public display of prisoners. And that perhaps that's the rationale for the -- that portion of the telegram. Do you know which convention and article you're thinking of? Can you be more specific? If you don't know, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't refer to a specific article, but I have it somewhere, but I can't think of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think you're referring to Article 13 of Geneva Convention III, which states that, likewise: "Prisoners of war must at all times be protected particularly against acts of violence, intimidation, insults, and public curiosity." You're not suggesting that that provision prevents aerial photography, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You are? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In that case, could I have P04308, e-court page -- let's just do it quickly, 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'm putting to you that this is what the concern was with aerial photography and why that telegram was sent. What you'll see is a photo of prisoners gathered at Nova Kasaba on the 13th of July at 1400 hours, right about the time of some of those intercepts, prisoners who we've agreed were killed, murdered, over the next four days. And you're telling the Court that you think the prevention of aerial photography was to stop exposing these people to public curiosity?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, how could I have prevented aerial photography? I'm just saying that aerial photography is part of a intelligence activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just stop, stop, stop [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every military in the world has to make efforts to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're not answering --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, you're not. My question was: Are you saying that prevention of aerial photography -- you just said to me that you thought the prevention of aerial photography was in line with the Geneva Conventions to prohibit exposing prisoners to public curiosity. I'm showing you a photo of prisoners who were murdered in the next four days, and you're telling me that this photo in your view would expose them to public curiosity, which is why it's important not to let photographs be taken.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In that I did not mean that that had to do with the article of Geneva Conventions that you quoted. I primarily meant every activity by uninvited persons among whom there is a majority of journalists more often than not and whose activity is intelligence activity. I didn't have in mind this specific article of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to go through them all because of time, but I'm sure as investigator for the Defence you're aware that we have photos of Sandici meadow from the air; at Pilica Dom with a truck shown in the back - that's P04308 at page 246; that we have a vehicle log and the testimony of the driver of the vehicle log, who said he was at Pilica Dom that day loading bodies; that we have photographs of Branjevo Farm, that's P04308, page 229, showing -- I'm impressed with how quickly the e-court's catching up; P4308 at page 229, this photograph. And I'm putting it to you, that's the purpose of prohibiting aerial photography: To hide the victims as they're detained, to hide the victims as they're transported, to hide the victims as they're murdered and as they're buried. And it wasn't successful.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What wasn't successful? Who wasn't successful?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The Main Staff, the VRS, was not successful in stopping aerial photographs of the people who were subsequently taken and killed, people at Nova Kasaba who were photographed there were murdered at Branjevo Farm and here in front of us we have an aerial photo of the Branjevo Farm murder site with bodies. I'm putting it to you that's what the prohibition of the aerial photographs was about?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can put it to me whatever you want. The Main Staff and the Army of Republika Srpska did not have the means by which they could prevent aerial photography.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, which is why you hide people inside buildings according to the telegram and move them to places like the Kravica warehouse or the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I did not try to do anything, and if my order was conveyed to Malinic, in the part where it says that people should be moved from open spaces, had a practical explanation. The ratio between the detainees and those who secure them was 20:1, if not more. And if such a situation, if night had fallen, the question is now whether any of my soldiers would have survived. The question is what would have happened? So that was a measure of efficiency, to secure the detainees with as little force as possible. There was no hidden agenda there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Of course then it could have just said secure the prisoners inside facilities before nightfall, not keep them from being exposed to aerial photography; right? That would have been a simpler way to put it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we have that order back? My memory is not photographic. I can't retain every single word. I can't remember what it says under which bullet point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What it says is, it's P00168, protected from sighting from the ground or the air.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From sighting from the ground and from the air, and I explained that in my statement. I explained why.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 65 ter 25399, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: A different topic. This is 1997 now. This is from the Main Staff -- excuse me, it's to the security administration of the VRS General Staff to you personally. And it's from General Tolimir. And you've seen this document before; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document at the Tolimir trial for the first time, and then I said that I had not seen it before and that I didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. You also said that doubtless it was sent to me but I don't remember receiving it at the time, right, in the Tolimir trial?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you can see that it was sent to me. However, can you display page 2, which will show us whether it was ever received by the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, we can go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On margin of the second page there should be a square stamp that belongs to the security administration, and it should display the date when a document was received. This is a customary procedure. Now I have my doubts as to whether this document was ever received by the security administration at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, if it's the received version but not -- the sent versions don't have received stamps. Now, this is about --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because of the time, very quickly, what General Tolimir here is recommending that this list of -- if we can go through it very quickly to the next page in both languages. And then the next page in the English, and the next page, sorry, in the English. All right. So because of the time I won't go through all of this. But what General Tolimir is saying is that this document has been received from - which he attaches - from the Dutch government and it's asking about what happened with these 239 male refugees from Srebrenica at Potocari. And the Dutch government are saying that they've asked for this information several times and have never received a response from the RS. And General Tolimir proposes that there be no written answer concerning this matter be sent to the Dutch embassy or government. And under no circumstances should any request regarding this document be replied to in writing, regardless of the content of the reply, because it could be used to legitimatise the list which was arbitrarily compiled by Mr. Nuhanovic. So you don't remember if you received this or not. What is Tolimir concerned about here? What is wrong with responding to the DutchBat request about what happened to these 239 people who were missing who were in Potocari? Or you have no idea whatsoever what this is all about?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I said when I saw this at the Tolimir trial that I had not received this. Anything I said about the document would be speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You also said this at the Tolimir trial, this is at T15795: "By the way, do you know what happened to this Ibro Nuhanovic? What became of him? He is referred to as having to do with compiling the list in this document?" Your answer was in 2011 on the 21st of June: "This is the first time I hear of Ibro Nuhanovic. I really have no idea. I have no clue who he is or what happened. I know nothing." Now do you know what happened to Ibro Nuhanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Karadzic's chief investigator -- who is Ibro Nuhanovic? What was his role?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit I have a problem with names, but if I remember well - I'm not sure though - somebody by that name or a similar name was a member of the negotiations commission. But then I might be completely wrong. You know the team that went to the Fontana Hotel. But I'm not sure by any means. That's the first thing that comes to my mind. If you could jog my memory with a document, I might be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. He was one of the Muslim civilian representatives of the people gathered in Potocari. And are you saying here today you don't know what happened to that man?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm saying I don't know what happened to that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you didn't follow the testimony of Petar Uscumlic, Mr. Karadzic's witness in this trial, who confirmed that Mr. Nuhanovic disappeared and agreed that he'd been murdered after being separated in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't follow Mr. Uscumlic's testimony because I have many other duties and I cannot follow everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well last question: In your role as investigator, do you know that the men separated in Potocari and taken away to Bratunac were murdered, subsequently murdered over the next few days?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were executions of prisoners of war, but all the details -- you asked me yesterday. On the 17th of July the people who were at Nova Kasaba were executed, you said. But how am I to know? I would have -- I would have to know who was at Nova Kasaba in the first place and then find out whether they were executed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This -- this --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to see some evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This was sent personally to you from Tolimir. Tolimir said: Do not respond to this in writing in any way or legalise this list because of people separated last seen at Potocari. What happened to those people, men?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know because at that time we didn't deal with these problems. What's the date when this was sent, by the way?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: February 27th, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sorry to go over the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] February 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you have some more questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a few. I'll cut it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- short. And I would tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would object, Mr. President. The witness has been unable to confirm any part of this document. And I also wonder what's the relevance of it with respect to his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It goes right to his ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would say it's relevant, it goes directly to his credibility, and he has not said that he did not receive it, that he doesn't recall. I think it goes to his credibility. It was sent personally to him from Tolimir and he hasn't disputed the authenticity of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We absolutely agree with you. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25399 receives number P6471, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce Charlie Jones from Vanderbilt University in the United States who has been a legal intern with our Defence team this summer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I want to ask you about an exhibit, a Defence exhibit, 1D00646. The "monologue of the 8th Operation Group of the ABiH." Now, this document was not admitted but I want to ask you a little bit about it. In this trial at T1378 His Honour Judge Kwon, the Presiding Judge, asked Mr. Karadzic: "What is this document about? Who prepared or produced this document?" And Mr. Karadzic responded: "Excellencies, this is a monologue, monograph of the 8th Srebrenica operational group," et cetera. And on the next page Mr. Karadzic said again: "Excellencies, this is a Muslim source, a monograph about their own army after the war. It is loaded into the EDS and e-court," et cetera. And His Honour, the Presiding Judge said: "Mr. Karadzic, I would take your word, but you're not giving evidence and we're not satisfied with the foundation of the document," et cetera. So just to bring you up to speed: We sent a letter to the Defence and said we would like to inspect the original of this document. And if we could just have the cover page in e-court. And we met with Mr. Sladojevic who brought a CD and told us that the Defence did not have an original, had no opportunity to provide it with us, and told us that this is all that their investigator got and couldn't tell us where it came from. So, first of all, could we zoom in on this, please, a bit on the 8, which looks to be of a different type-set. And the reason we asked about this is by chance we got this on a CD and we copied and pasted this PDF into a Word file, and I'd like to show in Sanction what happens when that is done. We'll copy and paste this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we go any further, could we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And if we could show on -- I don't know if we need to switch to Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let us switch to Sanction. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now we'll copy this PDF into a word document and the 8 changes to a 2, which now matches the type-set more. And the properties on the PDF say that it was created - and this is not an allegation - that it was created by a member of the Defence team when you look at the properties of the PDF. So my question is: As chief investigator, what is this document? Where did it come from? Why are we provided with it only on CD? And why does the 8 change to a 2 when the PDF is cut and pasted into a Word document and there we see what appears to be the original, unaltered - I'll put it that day - document. I know that's a compound question, but I would like you to explain this document and why we just saw what we saw.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document which is, in fact, a monograph of the 2nd Corps of the BH army and only partly of the 8th Operative Group, which later became the 28th Division, was obtained from a member of a -- a former member of the 28th Division. This document was on a CD and we used it as such. I'm not sure here if the 8 was changed into a 2. I don't think that this is any hocus-pocus. But simply we're talking about two operative groups. This is not only about the 8th Operative Group but about the overall organisation of the 2nd Corps during the war. There were operative groups and later I believe that it was in 1994 that they switched to divisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, okay, I'll stop you there because we're going a little astray. Who obtained this document, you or of the one investigators that you co-ordinate?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I obtained this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at the very beginning of my work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this also be redacted, this sentence. If the Trial Chamber needs more information, then I request that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't object to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Why were you not able --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why, very briefly, could you not get a hard copy of this "monologue"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We made great efforts to come by this monography, but still we were unable to. Our conclusion is that it was very soon called back because it did not suit the members of the Muslim people or the members of the BH army because it's -- also speaks about the war time --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- experience of the unit which also --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You answered the question, that you thought they would not want it available to -- made available. Okay. Well, the 8th OG is the one in Srebrenica. The 2nd OG is not in Srebrenica. If you say this was about both, why has the title of the monologue and all the contents been altered, clearly altered, to make it appear that the entire contents of the document apply to the 8th OG? And I'd like you to explain --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- why --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what was altered and where?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We just showed you how very clearly the cover here, 2nd Corps, 2nd Operativna Grupa in the original, and what was tried to be submitted to the Court and provided to us, if you happen to cut and paste it from the PDF into a Word file, it has been altered to read "8th Operational Group." Why was the title altered? And we can do it again if you want to see it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be the other way around?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, Your Honour. 2nd Operational Group altered to 8th Operational Group to make it appear as though it's all related to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No explanation. Is that what that means with the hand wave?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A hand wave can mean many things. This is about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- entire monography of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what it's about. I'm asking you why the cover was clearly changed from 2nd to 8th.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that and I didn't draw that conclusion. I am saying that the initial organisation of the 2nd Corps of the BH army --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was by operational groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll do it one more time. Watch your screen, please. We're going to take the PDF which says "8th Operational Group," which was what was tried to be admitted before this Court, 8th Operational Group; i.e., Srebrenica. That's what happens if you cut and paste it into a Word document. The layer on the top on the PDF disappears and you get the original.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a question for someone who is savvy in IT things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Let me ask --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You don't -- can't explain. I don't have much time. Let me ask you this: When you gave it to the Defence, when you got the CD and gave it to the Defence, is that what we saw, 2nd Operational Group, is that the form you gave it in?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Corps had more than one operational group. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. We're talking about this image. We got this and it was submitted to the Court on a CD. When you got the CD, brought it, and gave it to your colleagues on the Defence, is that what the image on the CD was and only that, 2nd Operative Group?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several images like this. I didn't deal with these details, especially with altering an 8 to a 2 or a 2 into an 8. I cannot say anything about that. But I can say that I don't have the expertise to do that nor did I do anything of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, who -- how did it -- I don't want to keep asking this. If you don't know, say you have no idea. How did it change after you got it from 2nd Operative Group to 8th Operative Group when it was tendered for admission, the image?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really unclear to me. I have very literally knowledge in this field, too little to be able to say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. When you handed it over -- presumably you looked at this document when you got it from your source. When you handed it over and you opened it up on the disc, did it say "2 Operative Group" just like we see there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interested in the content, what it says. As for the images, such as insignia, were of no interest to me. I was interested in the contents of their monography.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, okay --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In each monography you see the names of the people who made it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and you have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Savcic, if you could excuse yourself for a moment. There's something ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, could you explain to us about your basis that -- for your argument that the original should be the one which says 2nd Operation Group?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because if you look at them, you can very clearly see that the 8 is a completely different -- if we can bring the 8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether we can compare the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we can go bigger, expand on the 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In terms of typography and colour?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I have colour print-outs which make it much clearer than on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There -- there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 2nd Corps after this 2 we see a period, but we do not -- in the -- the Serbian would not put a period after 2nd Operation Group after the Arabic letter 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That I don't know. But you're correct, Your Honour. I hadn't noticed it. There's a period after the 8 but not after the 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're quite correct. Could we take a look at the print-out. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ordinal numbers in the Serbian language do not have additions or suffixes like in English, 1st, 2nd, et cetera. Instead of those, dots are used. However, if we look at the contents then there's no doubt that it's a monography of the 8th Operational Group. We're wasting time. This chapter is about the 8th Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we are talking about the cover page, this insignia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I don't think that this is the cover page. These are pages that mark chapters in that monography. For each operational group for each section there is such an inserted page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether it was a cover page or a chapter, new chapter page, do you agree that the Arabic letter 2 was altered to 8?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree, Excellencies. It is possible that they used one template for all operational groups and then they just changed the numbers. If it says "8th Operational Group," it means that they had at least eight such groups and it's the same template where you just graphically alter the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a separate matter. Whether this template -- this picture -- this image that we see in front of us was altered or not, that was the question. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. For my part it appears clearly to be altered, but I would like to -- since that's a very serious allegation, I would like to know from the Prosecution whether this -- whether there's evidence that this was altered by the Defence team afterwards or whether it was altered by the BiH army because that's a very serious allegation that Mr. Nicholls is making that it was the Defence that altered this. So is he able to say or not?
