Because if he is, then I want to -- I think this should be seriously investigated by our Defence team and I will do that, but if it's not, then the document should be admitted because it's clearly -- now we have provenance to admit the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what -- I think if we look back at the transcript is I've been asking for an explanation from their witness, their chief investigator - who received this - how it happened and why before I made any allegations and haven't made allegations. The -- and I'm not an expert, but the properties, as I said, on the PDF in the disc we got shows created by a member of the Defence team, and I said before that's not an allegation, that's just what it says. So I've been trying to get an explanation from their chief investigator about how this happened. And I don't think it should be on me to explain whether it was altered before or after they received it when it's their document that they tried to tender. I think they would know and their investigator should know. And it's only by chance that we noticed this when we were cutting and pasting that the 2 changed to an 8. So I'm not throwing any stones. I've been trying to get an explanation of how a document which is clearly altered was tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you can communicate to the Defence team who the author was in the property of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, they'll have it in theirs as well, their CD --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But I can communicate that to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I will show very simply how this is done. If I open a document with Fax Viewer, a TIF document, I have a tool to make notes in it, insert frames, and so on. If I open the same document in another programme, Document Imaging, then those additions are not there. If they had a template, they could save that template in one programme and then edit it using another, as Mr. Nicholls has shown. I have some documents here that are marked or annotated if opened in TIF, but if they opened in Document Imaging, you cannot see those changes. And that's this graphic editing, whereas the contents, it fully matches the 8th Operational Group. There's no doubt. And it is so comprehensive and goes to so much detail that nobody could make all that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not giving evidence about that. Why don't we just leave it there and continue with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I'll move on. I'll just say that in the document properties, responding to what Mr. Karadzic just said, with again the huge caveat that I'm not an expert in this and don't pretend to be and I'm not testifying, but the name of the -- this was on a CD. The name of the PDF creator was not the person mentioned in private session who this was obtained from or anybody else. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, whether we do this in front of -- with the witness or not, but I wanted to move the admission of the document now because I think we have enough provenance -- some of these issues as to the cover page will go to the weight. But now he's told us where he got this document from. It's been -- now -- the contents are relevant. So there is now no reason why the document can't be admitted in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would say that the provenance is still suspect and the fact that there has been a clear tampering on the cover page of the exhibit they sought to tender or changing of a number makes it inadmissible at this stage, just as it was at the beginning. It only adds to the inadmissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But it's just as likely if not more that the ABiH did this and made it into the 8th Operational than it is our Defence team, so I don't see why it should not be admitted without -- when the contents of the document, not the title page, is what's relevant and you've now had enough evidence from General Savcic as to the provenance of where he got that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that "just as likely" meets the standard, especially when the Defence can't even begin to explain why this is happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we can't explain because we don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls is putting a presumption that the Defence team tampered with evidence. As I'm sitting here right now, this is all a surprise to me. And if it was done by the ABiH when they were creating this document as a way of changing from 2nd Corps to 8th, that has nothing to do with the unreliability of the document. The contents, as Dr. Karadzic pointed out, deal exclusively with the 8th Operational Group and General Savcic has told us where he got this document from, so there is no reason why the document couldn't be admitted at this stage regardless of questions about the cover page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is not still satisfied with the provenance of the document. We do not find a basis to admit this document at the moment. Shall we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and just to respond to Mr. Robinson briefly. What General Savcic said at page 43 -- page -- end of page 42, start of page 43 is: "This document is, in fact, a monograph of the 2nd Corps of the ABiH army and only partly of the 8th OG group ..." And, Your Honour, for the record I would tender the two images just to be clear for the record what we've been discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to follow the transcript of today?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, there's no objection, but I think it's very incongruous for you to admit the cover page of a document without admitting the rest of the document but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, without this document, it's impossible to follow today's transcript at a later stage. That's the whole purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, that took much longer than I expected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I don't think that will be counted as your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are going to produce one sheet containing the two images?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that and show it to our friends and then upload it if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the Defence also wish to take a look at these images?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll assign a number for this image.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, do we have a 65 ter number for them yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not yet I don't think.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. So number for two images would be P6472, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. We'll collapse this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 25455.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is an easy one. This is your declaration regarding your -- regarding Milenko Zivanovic, the Drina Corps commander's refusal to testify. And this is public. Now, very briefly, this is your --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have it in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is no translation attached, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry that the original's not there which was probably attached to the filing, if I can get a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll ask you generally, when you spoke -- and I'm not cross-examining you about every word on this. When you spoke to Mr. Zivanovic, he refused to testify and you wrote that he explained the position by alleged threats from Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Europe and pointed out that there was a price on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why irrelevant, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because this is impeachment of General Zivanovic. It has nothing to do with the credibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Savcic, could you kindly take off your headphones once again. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. So we know there are rules for impeachment of witnesses. Those rules are that you put a statement to a witness: Did you tell General Savcic that there was a bounty on your head. And then the witness either says yes or no. If the witness says "yes," that's the end of it. If the witness says "no," the party has the option if they want to to call the person to whom the statement was made to impeach them in their rebuttal case if that hadn't been anticipated. So all those rules are being thrown out the window now and you're allowing the Prosecution to ask about witnesses who haven't yet come to testify to impeach those witnesses before they've even testified, and I don't see any basis for being able -- the Prosecution being able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson -- I'm sorry, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what rule exactly Mr. Robinson is speaking about, but I don't know of any rule that says that when an investigator spoke to a witness who's coming up I can't ask him what the witness told him. Mr. Robinson is trying to put forward some sort of convoluted procedure where we would have to -- having General Savcic, the chief investigator, who spoke to Mr. -- General Zivanovic and said he received death threats, not be allowed to ask him what those are, then put it to Mr. -- to General Zivanovic when he testifies were there these death threats, yes or no, and then re-call and go back and try to ask Mr. Savcic to explain what those were. He's filed a declaration saying that Mr. Zivanovic stated to him that there were death threats on his head, there was a price on his head, and Mr. Savcic continues to say it's his belief that Mr. Zivanovic was instructed not to testify. So I think I'm perfectly entitled to ask what these death threats were so that we know about them so I can decide whether and how to put them to Mr. Zivanovic if and when he testifies, and should be allowed to also ask who instructed him not to testify. And that seems to me very basic and I don't know why the Defence would think they should be -- that there's something wrong with them filing something with the Court saying the witness was subjected to death threats, and when they bring the witness here who took that -- wrote that declaration, I'm not allowed to ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This testimony may very well be completely inadmissible if General Zivanovic confirms the material, just like many times the Prosecution witnesses confirmed things that were written in reports of their interviews and that was not necessary for us to call the investigator to repeat what the witness had allegedly said to them. So the fact is that this is premature and is very -- may very well be that this testimony from General Savcic would be inadmissible. So it shouldn't be allowed at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As in the previous case, we agree with Mr. Nicholls. He's entitled to put those questions. Please go ahead. Mr. Savcic, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. What were the death threats to General Zivanovic that he told you about? Who was threatening to kill him if he came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me literally: There is a group of Muslim extremists in Vienna which put a price on his head, and it is said that whoever brought his head on a platter would receive that much gold. This is his problem about testifying here and that's why he doesn't want to appear before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did he say how he knew or who it was that were going to pay gold for his head on a platter in Vienna?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not insist on an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at the bottom of your declaration - I'm not going to ask you about your beliefs on whether those were justified or not, his reasons - but you said, and don't worry about the exact wording, that he'd been instructed to refuse to testify. How do you conclude that somebody had instructed General Zivanovic not to testify in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think that it should be verbatim translate -- presented. "I believe," he said, and it was out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct, that you believed he'd been instructed not to testify, so same question. What makes you believe that he'd been instructed not to testify by somebody or some people?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is no real reason that would prevent a man to appear as a witness, then there must be a different reason, another reason which may be imaginary or something else. This is my conclusion and I suggested that he should be called as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So just so I understand you. You couldn't think of any real reason why he wouldn't want to testify, so that was your basis for believing that he must have been instructed not to; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation was as follows: That I knew of the reasons. Actually, I didn't understand what the real reason was for which --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness received a wrong interpretation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that he didn't know for what reason the witness would have wanted to testify, so he cannot provide a correct answer based on an erroneous interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's what I was going to suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think you got a wrong interpretation. So if I understood you correctly, you weren't convinced by the death threats, you couldn't think of any "real" reason why he would refuse to testify. That was the basis for your belief that he must have been instructed not to testify; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're through, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency, but I do hope I will complete it before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, you were asked --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at P00168.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You wanted to say something about the heading of this document, but Mr. Nicholls kindly left it to me. Can you please tell us whether this is a printer -- teleprinter form or what did you want to say about the heading?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a teleprinter format. This was done on an ordinary typing machine, and as far as the heading is concerned, I wanted to say that the heading reads the IKM which stands for the forward command post of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. I wanted to say that. In formal terms, the forward command post of the protection regiment in the sector of Borike did not exist throughout the operation and it didn't exist for a very simple reason, for a single reason, because I was the only member of the command in that area and on that axis. So it was impossible to set up a command post which would consist of only one man. By definition, one knows what a command post is or what it should be. Second of all, this document, as you can see, was not registered anywhere, it was not signed. It sounds incredible to me that any of the communications guys would dare process such a document. I could speak to that Gojkovic. I could have agreed anything with Malinic, but it never occurred to me. I simply cannot understand, especially in view of my war authority that I enjoyed, that somebody would have dared to take a paper with my name on it without being sure that I was actually the author of the document. I don't think that anybody would have dared to process and send such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, is it customary that between P and lieutenant-colonel -- first of all, what was your rank at the time, were you a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1995 I was a lieutenant-colonel, and this is written as P Colonel without a full stop, as PPUK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since this is not a teleprinter format, what would be the reason for the lack of signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely don't know why. I don't know who would have done that. Just a while ago we were asking -- we were talking about the credibility of the monograph of the 8th OG. I have my doubts about that. And this is very similar to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about the contents of this document. You also tried to say that but then Mr. Nicholls delayed that for my additional questions. What did you want to say about the contents? What is the nature of the contents? Is there something illegal or unlawful in the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the contents of this document there is nothing unlawful. If you will allow me, I would like to go through the document bullet point by bullet point. Under bullet point 1 it says: "Prohibit access to all uninvited persons, taking photos of prisoners." In theory and in practice of any army uninvited persons are all those who are not members of a particular unit. There is no exception to that rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I interrupt you just for a moment. Do you know or do you remember, since you were near Zepa, whether the media were present during the evacuation of civilians from Zepa? What media and on what basis? Were they uninvited or were they invited and were given a permit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in Zepa our local media were present as well as representatives of some foreign media, but only those who were accredited and whose presence was approved during those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue. But briefly. Could you comment all the four bullet points.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a nutshell I draw your attention to the bullet point securing combat under the rules of the brigade, rules of the corps, and the strategy of combat. These measures are provided for as obligatory measures that had to be undertaken in all combat activities. They are even undertaken in peace time by all the militaries of the world. If I wrote this, if I forwarded this, in no event did this point to a plan or an intention to do something else to the prisoners, save for what is stated here. If anybody had sent this document to me, I would have done what it says here, i.e., that prisoners should be sheltered, that would be the end of it. As for the engagement of the military police, it is a normal task of the military police in war time to control certain sectors, movements through the men, and similar things. So all of these bullet points are absolutely in keeping with rules of combat, those that were in effect at that time. And they don't reveal any hidden agenda. Even as I read them today I can conclude the same. Unmanned aircraft has been mentioned here on several occasions. Let me share with you my personal experience. On several occasions I was targeted by enemy artillery on the co-ordinates that were provided by unmanned aircraft, especially by Croatian artillery. If I had any means, I would have neutralised such unmanned aircraft without any hesitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My last question about this document: Is there a teleprinter format? Did you ever see it? Is there anywhere a teleprinter format of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see the teleprinter format of this text. I don't know whether it's in existence anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If it existed, would that be the confirmation that it was dispatched?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, it would mean that the document was sent in its form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask for a document to be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Prosecutor, but it does arise from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we see the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, could we -- sorry, could we just see the ERN. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't activate my ELMO, but -- ah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did you receive this order by General Mladic which mostly refers to your protection regiment? It was sent on the 4th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber - it seems that there is no translation unless Mr. Nicholls can produce it from a hat - can you tell us how come the soldiers had to go to Han Pijesak to make telephone calls? How far were you from Han Pijesak? What were communication opportunities like at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distance between the staff and Han Pijesak is about 6 to 7 [Realtime transcript read in error "67"] kilometres. Most of the communication or road went through a densely wooded area. From July 1992 throughout the war we had occasional attacks on that road and ambushes were set by the enemy. I believe that this was issued on the 4th of July, 1995, immediately after the all-out attack which happened on the 26th of June and targeted the command post. What was envisaged here is a restricted movement procedure in order to have full control and prevent surprises.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By "staff," what did you mean, Mr. Savcic? You said: "... between the staff and Han Pijesak is about 67 kilometres."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was 6 to 7, Your Honours, the interpreter notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So 6 to 7 kilometres. "Staff" meant Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it meant Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did General Mladic issue an order for people to move in smaller groups and on foot to Han Pijesak, that the soldiers would be let to go there. Could they make private telephone calls from Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a post office was operational. I had just one telephone line, but that was not sufficient for all the soldiers to call their parents. And as for going there on foot, that was one of the security measures because the enemy could be discovered if one moved on foot. Vehicles are more easily ambushed than soldiers moving on foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure how he might tie it up, but I don't see how soldiers walking from Han Pijesak to Crna Rijeka to call their parents arises from my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are they not all related to the way in which telegrams could be sent, those communications?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't really -- it may be, that's why I said if he ties it up. But Crni Rijeka to Han Pijesak and walking there because it's dangerous to make a phone call, I don't see how that ties up at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Your Excellency, you are completely right, but another reason why I'm showing this document is going to be clarified with the next question of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do we know, General, that this was received at the command of the 65th Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the second page? On the second page in the lower left-hand corner there is a stamp that says "Command of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment," strictly confidential 3951, the 5th of July, so it does have a stamp of receipt. It arrived at the regiment and the commander has been made aware of it and takes measures in accordance with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us why this travelled from the 4th until the 5th and whether it has anything to do with the fact that this is not teleprinter either. How did this travel in order to arrive at headquarters only on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is regular mail. It goes once a day via courier from the staff administration, also at the protection regiment but they also work for the Main Staff. Very rarely it would happen that telegrams - it's only if they were extremely urgent - would be sent the very same instant when they were written up from the Main Staff to the protection regiment. In my practice it happened only once and that was the night between the 26th and the 26th [as interpreted] of June when sometime in the morning, around 4.00, the courier from the Main Staff brought me some intelligence that required urgent instantaneous action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted for identification, Excellencies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll mark it for identification. Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... were asked --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number D3926, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: MFI. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, no objection. Could I just see the original for a moment -- not the original but the copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about the fate of Mr. Nuhanovic. Did you have an opportunity to establish whether there was any personal revenge and whether some people suffered on that basis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Have a faith, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- how --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Have a faith. I'll show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does it arise from the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Because General Savcic was asked about Nuhanovic's testimony, and I have some document that is implying something that I can't say before General answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My objection was just leading. It was a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, what was the situation in terms of personal relations in relation to crimes on both sides in the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to that, I can say that in that area -- actually, that I was in that area from July 1992 onwards, so throughout 1992, 1993. Very often with my unit I was there in that part of the territory and I know that already in July -- sorry, in January 1993 a girl who worked at the command of the Zvornik, or rather, no, the Bratunac Brigade had accurate records. And until January 1993 there were already 1.200 casualties, Serb victims I mean, in that area. That is something that certainly had an influence and the Trial Chamber had an opportunity of visiting that area and seeing how short these distances are between Srebrenica, Bratunac, Milici. People mainly knew each other, in 80 per cent of all cases, and they knew who did what. So this possibility and this danger was always there, and in some cases it was actually materialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D43566, could we have that in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that document. Mr. Robinson, the Defence is going to upload the previous document which we marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could we get the number again of the last document? It cannot be located. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D43566. If necessary, it can be put on the ELMO. It's the last document and the last question and it should be in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is not available in e-court, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask for the ELMO then, please, just briefly. It's one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you tell the Trial Chamber and the participants what this is and what the date is?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can see well -- now, is this the 1st of March, 1995? Bulletin of security-related events, Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was signed by Milenko Karisik or someone signed it for Karisik; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone for Karisik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page. [In English] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the 8th of March. Could you please read the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The centre of public security of Zvornik" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The centre of public security of Zvornik submitted a supplement to the criminal report that the public security station in Skelani filed against a group of Muslims because they were -- there were grounds for suspicion to the effect that on the 10th of January, 1993, they committed a war crime over several civilians and torched several houses in Serb villages in the area of Skelani." The supplement to the criminal report pertains to Nuhanovic, Hasan from Srebrenica who is in the group of Muslims who fled from Srebrenica to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and there are grounds for suspicion that he participated in the above-mentioned crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there a crime on the 10th of January, 1993? Were you informed about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was informed. On the 7th of January, 1993, I was urgently sent from the Main Staff to the area of Bratunac because of the attack on Kravica. And immediately, a few days later, I was ordered to go on to Skelani because there were attacks there and the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was already under threat. I'm aware of the crimes committed in all Serb villages during those days, that is, east of Skelani, in the direction of Srebrenica. I remember now Jezero and some other villages. Right now I cannot recall all their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember this document, this telegram, of General Tolimir that was sent to you personally, as a matter of fact, and you were not sure that it had arrived? Do you remember that it is written there -- or should we actually call it up? That it is written there that this list was handed over to Ibro Nuhanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: By Ibro Nuhanovic, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ibro Nuhanovic and mentioned in that telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.text: If we can call this document. Mr. Nicholls certainly knows what number is it. Yeah, it is 65 ter 25399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit P6471.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be enlarged a bit, the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. In paragraph 3 under number 2 it says: "The attached list was delivered by Mr. Ibro Nuhanovic (born in 1943)." Is that what is written there? We are going to see that. Yes, yes, it is written there, it is written in the English translation too.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it says by Mr. Ibro Nuhanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who is the father of Hasan Nuhanovic, the person we mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have an AID document where it says that his father is Ibro Nuhanovic, but I'm not going to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there anything that I haven't tendered? Can somebody help me on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm totally lost as to where this is supposed to be going. Ibro Nuhanovic who I referred to in my cross, father's name was Hasan, according to the records. utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain. Ibro Nuhanovic is Hasan's son and his son is called Hasan, which is usual in our part of the world. And we have an AID document where Hasan Nuhanovic gave an interview to the AID in 1995. So that is the father, or rather, it is the grandfather, father, and grandson. At least one of them killed civilians -- Serb civilians, and if we are discussing their fate, we have to bear that in mind as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's irrelevant and just overwhelmingly offensive that -- what Mr. Karadzic is saying is that the murder of Ibro Nuhanovic was somehow justified by some other crime by -- committed by some other Nuhanovic I think is what he's trying to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not justified. I'm not justifying anything. I'm just trying to have us understand whether it was the state that was killing people or whether killings happened because of revenge. I just want us to understand. I'm not justifying anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kos. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.
