utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you will be aware of this already, but before you commence your evidence, Mr. Kos, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence we have here at the International Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you, as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kos. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kos.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to my Defence team in the form of an interview?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up 1D09591.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side please note whether this is the statement you gave to my assistant?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, this is that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read and sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please make a pause between my question and your answer for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page for him to identify his signature, the last page in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: This is my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, the answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I seek to tender this statement under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3927, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out a short summary of the statement given by Mr. Franc Kos in English. [In English] Franc Kos, a Slovenian national, was a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the Army of Republika Srpska in July 1995. The 10th Sabotage Detachment participated in the events after the fall of Srebrenica on three occasions. On 11th of July, 1995, they entered Srebrenica and helped secure the town. On 13th of July, 1995, they went to the warehouse at Kravica where Muslim prisoners had been killed. And on 16th of July, 1995, they went to Branjevo Farm, where they participated in the execution of Muslim prisoners from Srebrenica, prisoners of war. During his time at the Kravica warehouse, Mr. Kos observed about 20 corpses outside the warehouse. He was told that a Muslim prisoner of war had grabbed a gun from a guard and started shooting and that the prisoners had been killed when those guarding them returned fire. While they were at the Kravica warehouse, one member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment threw grenades into the warehouse. Mr. Kos did not see any corpses in the warehouse but estimated that the warehouse could hold no more than 120 prisoners. Mr. Kos personally participated in the execution of prisoners at Branjevo Farm. He estimates that approximately 350 men were shot at Branjevo Farm on 16th of July, 1995. They were told that the prisoners had to be shot because they were war criminals. Mr. Kos and the members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment never had the intention to destroy the Muslims as a religious group in whole or in part. The 10th Sabotage Detachment was made up of men from different religious and national groups. Mr. Kos has been convicted of crimes against humanity by the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and sentenced to 35 years in prison. He and the two other members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment were acquitted for genocide. And that is the summary. At that moment, I do not have questions for Mr. Kos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As you have noted, Mr. Kos, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written witness statement. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, let me pick up where Mr. Karadzic left off, that you were convicted of crimes against humanity by the state court. Zoran Goronja and Stanko Kojic were also convicted of crimes against humanity for their participation in the Branjevo Farm executions, weren't they, in the same trial as you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And Vlastimir Golijan, who was another member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment at Branjevo Farm, pled guilty in the state court for the Branjevo Farm executions, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And Marko Boskic also pled guilty to the Branjevo Farm executions in the state court?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, but later on he denied some facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. And Drazen Erdemovic was convicted of murder by this Tribunal; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And Aleksandar Svetkovic is currently under arrest in Israel and waiting to be extradited to Bosnia, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So of the eight members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment who were at Branjevo Farm, six have been convicted and one is currently under arrest. There's only one who hasn't been arrested yet and that's Brano Gojkovic; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, let's go straight to Branjevo Farm on the 16th of July, 1995. You went there that day and you had your own personal combat set with 150 bullets in it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my personal combat set.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you told Mr. Karadzic's lawyer in your interview that you also had a reserve personal combat set; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, but it was in my trunk, that is, an ammunition case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. A combat set has 150 bullets in it; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes. These are four clips in the wrap and one fastened to the rifle. Each clip holds 30 rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And each of the other seven members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment who you were with also would have had a personal combat set and a reserve combat set, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, they had their personal combat sets, and there was only one ammunition case in the trunk. I only saw it when we arrived at the Branjevo Farm. When you go into action, you always carry reserve ammo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that reserve crate in the back of the van had 1200 automatic rifle bullets in it, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the standard quantity in a crate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And in the back of the van there was also an M84 machine-gun that had its own crate of 1200 bullets; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that M84 machine-gun was used to kill some of the prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, for the first group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Stanko Kojic, who's also known as Stanko Sevanovic [phoen], he had a handgun with him that he used to kill some of the prisoners too; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, Stanko Kojic had his personal pistol M57 TT, calibre 7.62 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your interview with Mr. Karadzic's lawyer you said that you only used about four clips of ammunition, so about 120 bullets; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, four clips and the fifth was half empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And you said - this is at page 47 in English and the B/C/S page 21 - that: "I didn't use additional charges. I don't know about the others." So you don't know how many of all that other ammunition that was at Branjevo Farm that day was used by the other members of your unit; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can only speak about myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, there was another unit of about 10 to 12 soldiers from Bratunac who came to the farm during the afternoon, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes. They arrived when we were done executing the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And they had -- that unit had their own weapons and their own ammunition; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in line 19 "when we were done" is not a good translation. "When we seized" or "when we stopped" would be better. "When we were done" implies that we had completed the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And this unit from Bratunac also abused some of the prisoners, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you describe what they did to those prisoners before shooting them?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Well, when they came to the farm we were sitting and they first started yelling at us - how shall I put it? - that we were impertinent, irresponsible, cowards, traitors because we had stopped shooting the prisoners. And then they started taking the prisoners to the field. They singled out one and chased him around with a metal bar. And there was another on whom they took out their anger, beating him and so on. I suppose they knew him from before. We were sitting round and watching, the whole group, the entire group from the 10th Sabotage Detachment that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to play you a short video and get your comments on it. If I can play Exhibit P4306 starting at 5 minutes and 4 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: "11.04, recognise the farm ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can just pause there for a moment, 5 minutes and 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters haven't been provided with a transcript of that and the quality is poor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question and answer, please. It was overlapped with the interpreter's notation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, if you could just repeat your answer. I asked you if you recognised this location.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. It's the Branjevo Farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we could keep playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: "... search for shell casings. It's Thursday, the 30th, it's 1430, here we are still at the [indiscernible] farm, and we are now near the garages, if you look across the meadow. If we now walk this meadow to look for spent cartridge cases purely on the surface of this ploughed field, and we've marked those that we've found with a yellow marker. Measurements and -- measurements of the area in which we've found cartridges and the number of cartridges I'll provide when I walk there."

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I could pause there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So what we were just looking at there was the path where the prisoners walked towards the killing site; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that's at 6 minutes, 15 seconds. We can keep playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: "Okay. I've now walked about 25 to 30 metres to the rear of this garage area, and I'm standing more or less in the middle of the track that we cut when we walked down. And all the yellow markers can be seen stretching across the field. We've walked the field for maybe 200 metres, but as I say the proper measurement will be provided. "Okay. Here I am. I've walked on a few wards. And now I just give an idea of what it is exactly that we found that we were looking for. Exactly this type of thing, and this type of thing here. "Okay. I'm now maybe 3 -- 300 metres or so further out along this ploughed field from the back of those garages. And this area here, and this one and ones over there and panning back, this is the -- more or less the extent of any numbers of shells, although there is one right out there. Incidentally, we've found three different types of shell casing, shells that looked like machine-gun shells, AK shells, and one pistol shell."

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, the area that the investigator has been walking over and filming the cartridges, that's the area of the execution site, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you heard or he pointed out that there were M84 cartridges, automatic rifle cartridges, and a pistol cartridge. That's consistent with what you've said, that there were automatic rifles and M84 and Stanko Sevanovic had a pistol; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, only those were not M48 rifle cartridges but rather M84 machine-gun cartridges, whereas M48 is an old rifle also known as Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And just where the camera stopped here, this is the spot where the investigator said the cartridges basically ran out. So we're at this image here at 8 minutes and 22 seconds. That's the edge of the execution site there, right, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: That's not the edge of the execution site. I can explain. This is the so-called field which was ploughed. While the land was tilled, the cartridges were probably moved. When you plough, then the cartridges can be scattered all over the field. And the first executions from the M84 machine-gun when about 20 people were executed took place by this large bush in this slight depression. That was the only group that was executed with an M84 machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So the executions started a bit further down the field where we can see those -- the trees on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, in this depression down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If I can have P4305 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What you're about to see, Mr. Kos, is an aerial image of Branjevo Farm on 17 July 1995, the day after the executions. And you can see there the bodies of the prisoners that are still on the surface are -- stretch almost back to the garage; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, but just a moment. This photograph was not taken on the 17th of July. This one was taken on the 16th because as of 700 hours on the 17th of July, machines were being used there. Now, either this photograph is wrong or all the witnesses in the BH state court lied. On the 17th they said that they were burying the bodies at the Branjevo Farm. And if you could show the admin building, you will see a bus parked there. That bus transported the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kos, I don't think there's any dispute here that on the 17th of July those bodies that you can see were in the process of being buried. We can agree on that, right, that the burials happened on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you now about the number of buses that came to the Branjevo Farm on the 16th of July with prisoners on board. Now, do you remember in May 2010 you were interviewed by Mr. Tomasz Blaszczyk, an investigator with this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you understood that the purpose of that interview was to find out about your role in the Srebrenica operation, and particularly at Branjevo Farm?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you understood the seriousness of the inquiries that were being made and how important it was to tell the truth during that interview?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 25482 in e-court. Page 90 in the English and page 64 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And what you're about to see, Mr. Kos, is a transcript of your interview with Mr. Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can have page 64 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you can see there, Mr. Kos, in the transcript you say: "Up until the fifth or sixth bus, people who were brought did not have either their eyes or their hands tied, they were not blindfolded, and they didn't -- they were not hand tied." You were then asked how many buses came after that sixth bus and you said: "All together, at the period of time that we were up there, some ten buses arrived. With the 11th bus, some other people also came, and they with that 11th bus some soldiers came who immediately took people out and took them to the field and they killed them on their own ..." And if we go over to the next page in English, you say: "When they arrived I think that we after that shot only one bus of people and they continued to shoot the others ..." So in this interview you said up to the 11th bus you were shooting and then the other unit is the unit from Bratunac, they took over and they shot the other buses; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: I can't say just yes or no. I have to explain. I as a participant in all that, I never considered those acts that I had committed because I knew I would be arrested sooner or later, so I didn't give it a second thought. When I was arrested, I did give an interview but I never reflected on the number of buses. Later on, when I saw the number of buses, when I observed the executions and what was going on, I realised that not more than seven and a half or eight and a half buses arrived at Branjevo. The first bus when it arrived and when it was said that they were POWs that had to be executed, and when I returned to the place from which the buses came, and when half of the men were taken out of the buses, that half was executed with an M84 machine-gun and a lot of them were wounded. And about 25 people were then executed with automatic rifles. Those people were tied, the first group. The second group an argument broke out. I didn't hear what Gojkovic said to Erdemovic and Erdemovic then replied: "I can't do that." They quarrelled and then they left. Then I approached Erdemovic and I told him -- Erdemovic's nickname was Djino. I told him: "Djino, shut up, otherwise they'll kill us too. Can you not see what's going on?" And then we went back. And later on when I saw how many wounded there were, I approached the three or four that -- whose intestines I saw protruding from their stomach, they were wailing and crying, then I approached them and shot them in the heads to kill them. And then I said: "People, we can't do it like this." Then somebody said: "We can't do it this way. We will execute them in groups of ten." That's what happened with the second bus. When the third bus arrived, it occurred to somebody, I don't know who it was, to ask money from them. They asked them if they had money or if they had relatives abroad. They singled out a lad to tell them whether he had money. And when the fourth bus arrived that lad was still there, or rather, when the fifth bus arrived I was sitting in one of those buildings and there was a man there. He was one of the detainees. He was a butcher in Srebrenica, that's what he told me. I had a word with him while some two groups were taken to be executed by the other members. When the sixth bus arrived we stopped shooting people. I know when I returned and when the sixth bus arrived somebody said that we had to hurry-up because some people wanted to break through and we were told that nobody must remain alive. It's a bit bizarre, but then I realised that there was a way out. I said: "I can't go on." We were thirsty, we were hungry, we went up to that building and we sat down there. At that moment another bus came and those people who continued executing the prisoners got out of the bus. We were tired and somebody didn't like the fact that we shot short bursts of fire into groups of ten people and that we shot them in the back of the head. Somebody must have been in a hurry and we obviously didn't do things quickly enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So as you sit here today, is it your evidence that you made a mistake when you were interviewed when you said that you shot up to 11 buses and then another unit took over and did the remaining buses? That was a mistake when you said 11 buses, was it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: I'm not saying this today [as interpreted]. I testified to the same effect when I testified in the BiH court. I provided the same statement when I testified on my own behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No, I understand that. But I'm asking you in 2010 when you gave an interview to Mr. Blaszczyk, you said that you shot up to 11 buses and then that the other unit took over and shot the remaining ones. So you've changed your testimony now or you've changed your evidence from 11 plus the other unit shooting some more down to seven. You've changed it; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay if we can have 65 ter 25481 in e-court. Page 33 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it's not that important; however, on line 12 the witness said -- [In English] "I'm not saying this only today." "Only" is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, you said just on the previous page you provided the same statement when I testified on my own behalf. You were interviewed by the Prosecutor at the state court before you testified, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see in this interview which is on the screen in front of you, we can go to page 33 in both -- you can see there in this interview you said you counted up to seven buses. And then after that the buses started to come quicker and quicker. So when the state court prosecutor interviewed you, you said you counted up to seven and then there were more buses that came quicker and quicker. So that's another different answer from what you're saying today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Just a moment. There's something missing here. I said, or rather, Erdemovic said 1200 in the first statement provided to Tomasz Blaszczyk. I never mentioned the number of people either to Tomasz Blaszczyk or here. It was Erdemovic. Erdemovic stated that there were 1200 men --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Kos. One second.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: -- and now I'm looking at the figure 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No, one second. Just above that we're talking about the buses, the number of buses, not the number of people. We'll come to that. All I'm saying is in this interview you said you counted up to seven. "We were down there another hour and a half but the buses were coming quicker and quicker later." Now, that's a different answer about the number of buses than you gave Mr. Blaszczyk and it's a different number than what you've said here today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I have to intervene. It doesn't say "faster and faster." Perhaps this changes the meaning and perhaps this confuses the witness. It doesn't say "faster and faster."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Perhaps things got confused here. I said that they started shouting that we had to execute them faster and faster. This may be the source of the confusion. When the sixth bus arrived, we were told that we were proceeding too slowly, that we should go faster. And another group arrived, so another bus followed. Two buses arrived almost simultaneously. We slowed down to the extent that two other buses came in. That's why probably someone meant that it should go faster and faster. Either it was mistranslated or wrongly recorded. When the sixth bus arrived, we received an order to proceed faster and then we stopped. We didn't continue. Another group took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, maybe you can read out, Mr. Kos, starting from line 10, if you can read that out in the original language and we'll listen to the translation and see if there was a mistake. You see where it starts at line 10?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If you could read out those three lines.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: I think that this part -- yes. "It's a shame. I counted up to seven, because in the first five or six buses the people were tied up and then the sixth bus came in." It matches. I said "seven buses," that is, six buses and a seventh and the eighth was half full. Overall, we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Kos --

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: -- a bus and another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- can I stop you there. Can you read out, no commentary, just what it says in lines 10, 11, and 12 just word for word what that says.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Very well. "I think it's a shame for me to say this. I counted up to seven. I counted to seven and later perhaps -- perhaps for another hour and a half we were down there, but the buses kept on coming quicker and quicker."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No "quicker and quicker," only one "quicker ."

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, my point is, Mr. Kos, that's a different answer than what you told Mr. Blaszczyk and it's different to what you've said today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean. What you mean when you say "different"? I told you, the events happened a long time ago and then in 2010 at first I couldn't remember all the details, I couldn't remember everything. And then I started reflecting on things. If I had been thinking about that, I would have had psychological problems and I did have them for the first year and a half. That's when I was popping pills. And then when I started thinking about what happened, how things happened, how many there were, then I remembered how things transpired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's move to something related but slightly different. You said in your interview with Mr. Karadzic's lawyer, this is at page 42 in the English and 19 in the B/C/S, that there were only two buses and they were rotating and bringing the prisoners from the school to the farm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I want to read you just three very short pieces of evidence in this case and then I'll ask you a question. This is from the testimony of one of the survivors of the Branjevo Farm executions. It's Exhibit P4342 and T3040 in his prior testimony from the Krstic case. And he's talking about being led out of the Kula school, and he says: "As we were leaving the school building, they told us to line up against a wall, put our hands behind our backs, and this is where our hands were tied. Three buses were parked there and we climbed on to the second bus. There were three of us sitting in one row of seats and once the buses were filled up they left." And then he goes on to describe how the convoy of three buses arrived at the Branjevo Farm at the same time. Now, the second piece of evidence is from the second survivor of the Branjevo Farm execution, Ahmo Hasic, and this is from Exhibit P354, where he says he remembered being brought out of the Kula school with other prisoners and being put on two buses that went to the Branjevo Farm at the same time. So we've got a convoy of three buses and a convoy of two buses from the evidence of the two survivors. Now, this is what Drazen Erdemovic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can have P6454 in e-court. Page 1 in the English -- actually, page 2 in the English and 1 in the B/C/S. My apologies, 6451.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And what this is, Mr. Kos, is an interview with Drazen Erdemovic that was published on the 22nd of March, 1996, so only about eight months after the Branjevo Farm executions. And you can see in that article, it's in the second column in the original, where Drazen Erdemovic says there were five buses with logos of Centrotrans and Drinatrans who were driving civilians to the farm. So isn't it the case that there were actually five buses bringing prisoners to the farm that day. There was a convoy of three buses that would come at one time and then there was a pair of buses that would come separately. And these two groups were rotating for the whole time you were there, ferrying prisoners from the Kula school to the execution site?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: I can't confirm this. I can't answer. It was a long time ago --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You can't --

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: A moment, a moment. If there had been five buses, as you say, first five and then three in a column --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What I'm saying is --

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: -- we would not have had time --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What I'm saying is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, he should be allowed to finish his answer, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm clarifying the question for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm saying there's five in total. There's a group of three and a group of two and those two groups rotate. Now, 18 years later you can't exclude that there were five buses operating that day, can you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: I can't tell you how many buses there were. I was not in the Kula school. I was not in Pilica -- actually, it's one and the same. There is only a 3-and-a-half-kilometre distance between the two as far as I could see. How many buses there were and what make they were I really can't remember as I sit here today nor can I answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to something slightly different. You said -- or you saw an officer, a VRS officer at the Branjevo Farm that day who you later learned was Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that when the trial here in The Hague started, when the lieutenant-colonel was put on trial. I learned that he was the officer who was at Branjevo, but I personally didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But when you saw him on trial you recognised that that was the man you saw at Branjevo Farm that day, that was the officer you saw?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. The -- are you asking me about the officer who had brought us there or the officer who told us that we should execute people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sorry, let me clarify. The officer who told you you should execute people, that was Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: I can't confirm that that was Vujadin Popovic because I don't know that officer. I can describe him. He was tall, his hair was not grey, his complexion was fair, and he was aged between 40 and 45. That was the man who told us that we had to execute people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in your --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness said that his hair was not completely grey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But there's no dispute that the officer who told you to execute these prisoners was a VRS officer; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, in your interview with Mr. Karadzic's Defence lawyer, you also said that you saw Dragan Obrenovic at Branjevo Farm on the 16th of July, 1995. Now, that's the first time you've ever mentioned Dragan Obrenovic's [Realtime transcript read in error "Erdemovic"] name in connection with these events, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, for transcript, are we talking about Erdemovic or Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 15 should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kos, is it right that you told Mr. Karadzic's Defence lawyer that you saw Dragan Obrenovic at Branjevo Farm?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If you're not sure or if you can't remember if you saw Dragan Obrenovic, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, he was up there but he arrived in his own vehicle, but he left in no time. Once we arrived there, he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. You didn't know who Dragan Obrenovic was at the time, did you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, is it reflected in his interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At page -- could you give me the page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I believe it's page 26 in the English. It says: "And the officer who had brought us there, Dragan Obrenovic, was still present."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So at the time on 16 July, you didn't know the name of the officer who led you to the Branjevo Farm, did you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: The officer who had brought us to Branjevo, and he was in a red Kadett vehicle, was not Dragan Obrenovic. Dragan Obrenovic had a red Golf car and that was his personal vehicle, and he was in front of the Opel Kadett, and he was already there at Branjevo when we arrived. When we arrived, he turned around in his car and he left. He was a younger officer at the time and his behaviour was rather arrogant. He was arrogant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go into private session for one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, in 2004 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: In 2004 you were interviewed by an investigator with the Slovenian police, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that was the first time that you had been interviewed formally by anyone about the events at Branjevo Farm; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: How do you mean "formally"? As a suspect or to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I just mean it's the first time somebody had sat down with you and asked you to explain exactly what happened at Branjevo Farm. Not as a suspect or formally as a witness. It's just the first time you sat down with someone and they asked you to explain those events.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And this might be an obvious question, but you'd agree that your recollection about the events at Branjevo Farm would have been much fresher, much better, ten years ago when you gave that statement?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And we can agree that it wasn't in any way whatsoever in your interests to inflate or exaggerate the number of prisoners who were killed by your unit at Branjevo Farm, was it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 25487 in e-court. Page 1 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What you're about to see, Mr. Kos, are the notes of the investigator who interviewed you in March 2004. And we can see there he's noted down correctly your personal details and he's also noted correctly the false identification papers that you had with you at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if you read down a little bit, he's correctly noted down the circumstances under which you joined the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the manner in which you were arrested and spent time in solitary confinement; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go over to the second page in both English and B/C/S. I'll just finish with this document, Mr. President, in the next minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You can see there he's correctly noted down the circumstances under which you escaped prison and then ended up joining the VRS. He's got that right, hasn't he?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Just a moment, let me read it. Let me just read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, my question was, I'll just remind you: He wrote down accurately the circumstances under which you escaped prison and then you joined the VRS? He's got that right, hasn't he?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, on the whole it's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see he's got the names of the commanders of the 10th Sabotage Detachment Zoran Manojlovic and then Milorad Pelemis. They're both correct, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And then if you look a little bit further down, maybe go over to the next page on the B/C/S, and he correctly noted that on 16 July 1995 you received an order to go with seven members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment to the Branjevo Farm. That's also correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes -- well, no, actually. No one mentioned Branjevo. No, that's not correct. No one member of the group knew where we were going. We were said [as interpreted] that we were supposed to guard the prisoners. Nobody mentioned Branjevo or Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But he's correctly recorded that you and seven other soldiers did go to Branjevo Farm that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And we see there that he's written down that you estimated approximately 1.000 Muslims were killed at Pilica that day. So he's written down your estimate accurately there too, hasn't he?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: That's not correct. It says here 50 buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the number. He wrote down: "According to his estimation, approximately 1.000 Muslims were killed at Pilica that day." So in 2004 that was your estimate, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Even then I said that Erdemovic stated that there had been 1.000 to 1200 people. I never said that we executed 1.000 to 1200 people. I always said that that number was the estimate of Drazen Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But that's what you told the Slovenian investigator, wasn't it, during this interview? You mentioned the figure of approximately 1.000 Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS
utterances.text: Yes, but I referred to Erdemovic's statement there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This might be a good place to stop, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn for today and continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. Mr. Kos, you are advised not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony while you are giving testimony. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of August, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.52 p.m.,
